A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VirSci research. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite the changed title, formatting and organization.

before.justification: V1 reports original comparisons with AI Scientist, team-dynamics experiments, component ablations and novelty-metric validation using LLM and human assessments (Table 1, Section 4 and Appendix F).

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds cross-domain simulations, HypoGen comparisons, human ratings and further ablations (Table 1, Sections 4–5 and Appendices B–D).

M1.justification: The five-stage pipeline, invitation mechanism and self-review remain. V2 adds topic-discussion restart when consensus fails and permits uninterested agents to leave (Section 3.2). Its idea-generation prompt also drops the separate Existing idea field. The inter-/intra-team terminology largely reframes existing collaboration.

E1.justification: V2 expands beyond computer science by evaluating interdisciplinary collaboration using Open Academic Graph 3.1, covering fields including physics, chemistry and biology. It adds cross-domain team-dynamics and database experiments plus biomedical output examples. The original computer-science coverage and NanoGPT comparison remain.

E2.justification: V1 Table 1 compares VirSci only with AI Scientist. V2 Table 1 adds HypoGen under GPT-4o, LLaMA3.1-8b and LLaMA3.1-70b, substantially broadening the comparison to include another multi-agent scientific-idea system.

E3.justification: V2 changes metric normalization from a database-wide mean to a publication-year mean and expands metric validation from 100 to 200 abstracts. New protocols include blinded human comparisons on novelty, feasibility and effectiveness, HypoGen with 12 discussion turns, and OAG temporal filtering using 2010/2020/2023 boundaries. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds database-use ablations, sequential-versus-random speaking-order tests, alternative collaboration-weight increments and LLaMA3-versus-LLaMA3.1 sensitivity analysis. Existing component ablations expand from five turns to results across one through seven turns. It also expands metric validation and adds two biomedical feasibility case studies (Section 5; Appendices C–D).

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging experiments over 20 runs. For metric validation, v2 newly specifies three LLM reviews and three independent human assessments per abstract, with averaged scores (Appendix C). V1 does not specify this review replication; the disclosure does not establish an increase in simulation runs.

E6.justification: Existing AI Scientist/VirSci Table 1 scores and five-turn ablation entries remain unchanged. V2 adds HypoGen, human, OAG and supplementary results; GPT-4o human novelty scores are 5.24/4.94/4.78 for VirSci/AI Scientist/HypoGen. Validation correlations change from 0.59/0.51 to 0.57/0.52 for LLM/human assessments under revised validation conditions. The stated diversity optimum is also qualified to include 75%.

T1.justification: The definition of metric normalization changes from a whole-database mean to a same-publication-year mean, altering the normalized quantities entering ON (Section 4.1). The ON product/ratio formula and existing prompt/self-review equations remain substantively unchanged, including equations moved from v1 Appendix E. No new theorems or proofs appear.

C1.justification: The central claim that collaboration improves scientific idea generation remains. V2 reframes novelty around the real-data scientific ecosystem and inter-/intra-team communication, and broadens explicit superiority claims beyond single-agent approaches. Its abstract and conclusion shift emphasis from emergent social behavior toward investigating collaboration mechanisms.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of database grounding, speaking-order effects, exploration and cross-domain/backbone consistency. Appendix A adds a data-leakage defense based on claimed inability to reproduce original abstracts, while Appendix D presents biomedical abstract pairs as feasibility evidence. The single-domain limitation is removed; the limitation concerning realistic concurrent multi-team collaboration remains in Section 7.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds OAG filtering and author-profile reconstruction instructions, identifies the default backbone, and documents HypoGen and human-evaluation settings. It clarifies AMiner accounting as 85,217 past plus 92,980 contemporary papers, rather than establishing an underlying dataset expansion. The code-access target changes, while v1's preprocessed-data link and exact GPT-4o snapshot identifier are omitted.

R1.justification: V2 substantially revises positioning by engaging ResearchTown and HypoGen and distinguishing VirSci through dynamic collaboration and real scientist/network data. It also expands exploration–exploitation, scientific-measurement and dataset literature. This extends the argument beyond v1's predominant contrast with single-agent AI Scientist.

P1.justification: The introduction, contributions and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Metric validation gains a main-text section, ablations and discussions become separate sections, experimental details move into Appendix B, and self-review details move into the main methods. The title, author/affiliation block, terminology and appendix organization also change.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a different page format, typography and running headers. Table 1 gains grouped human-evaluation columns and baseline rows; component tables expand across discussion turns. Team-dynamics figures gain OAG panels, and new topology, exploration, backbone and biomedical-example figures appear. Updated human-validation results are displayed in both the main text and appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central collaboration claim by addressing v1's acknowledged single-domain limitation, adding a relevant multi-agent comparator and blinded human comparisons, and testing database and discussion-design choices. Expanded, better documented metric validation also strengthens the evaluation. These gains outweigh losses in data-access/model-version details and the limited evidential value of the new feasibility examples, which do not validate their generated experimental claims.
